lead: Pellevé is a monopolar radiofrequency (RF) wrinkle-treatment system made by Ellman International, operating at 4 MHz.[1][2] It is an in-office treatment in which a handpiece warms the skin to a therapeutic temperature so that existing collagen contracts and new collagen is laid down, with the aim of smoother, tighter-looking skin on the face, neck, around the eyes and on the hands.[1][4][7] It was one of the RF devices that followed the introduction of Thermage in 2002.[4]

A 2011 clinical article describes the procedure as delivering continuous monopolar RF energy rather than pulsed heating and repeatedly bringing skin to therapeutic temperatures until maximal contraction is obtained, which the author reports gives visible results over all treated areas painlessly and with no downtime.[4] A 2010 French review describes the Ellman 4 MHz principle and notes that it can be combined with fillers and botulinum toxin within certain time limits.[7]

Published studies include a 17-patient facial study, a 31-patient hand-wrinkle study and a 12-patient periorbital cohort, alongside registered studies of face and neck wrinkles.[1][2][3][5][6] All are small, and the facial and periorbital studies have no described control arm.

chain: Monopolar 4 MHz RF warms the dermis to a therapeutic temperature
Collagen contracts and new collagen synthesis is stimulated
Wrinkles soften and skin looks tighter over weeks
angle.text: Pellevé treatments are used to soften fine wrinkles and tighten mild skin laxity on the face, neck, eye area and hands without surgery or downtime. Studies report visible improvement across a series of sessions, with some measurable brow lift after periorbital treatment.

paras: Pellevé delivers continuous monopolar RF rather than pulsed heating; the 2011 article's author describes the approach as treating all areas until contraction is seen and as comfortable for patients.[4] A 2012 paper reviews the science of RF-induced collagen synthesis alongside its clinical series.[1] The French review of cosmetic radiofrequency says high-frequency electric current generates heat in subcutaneous tissues sufficient to break collagen fibres and allow neocollagen synthesis, permitting skin resurfacing, improved tone, and delicate reshaping of facial volumes.[7]

Wikipedia's article on RF skin tightening states that RF heats skin to stimulate collagen, elastin and hyaluronic acid production, that the dermis should reach about 67 degrees Celsius, and that delivering RF until that temperature is reached optimizes outcomes; it notes that penetration depth depends on electrode configuration (monopolar, bipolar or unipolar).[8]

The 2012 study of 17 patients received six treatments over about five months: two sessions 15 days apart, two a month apart and two two months apart. Assessment was by the treating physician and by patients comparing with baseline photographs. Two weeks after the first treatment patients noted an average 25 to 30 percent improvement, and just before the sixth treatment the physician noted an average 50 percent improvement and patients rated a 48 percent self-improvement.[1]

A multicenter study enrolled 31 women with a median age of 56 at two centres for hand wrinkles and described itself as the first to assess hand laxity improvement with RF. One hand was randomised for treatment and three treatments were given at two-week intervals. At 90 days 89 percent of patients showed visible improvement on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale, with 50 percent visibly improved and 39 percent markedly improved. Patients reported mild to moderate discomfort and no adverse events were reported.[2]

A prospective cohort of 12 patients aged 30 to 60 with minimal laxity and shallow wrinkles used a Canfield Reveal imager to document periorbital change after one or two sessions. Average eyebrow lift was 2.05 mm and upper eyelid crease elevation 0.98 mm immediately after treatment, and brow elevation at eight weeks averaged 3.52 mm.[3]

The hand study reported mild to moderate discomfort and no adverse events, and the 2011 article describes the procedure as painless with no downtime.[2][4] Wikipedia's RF skin tightening article, describing RF devices more broadly, notes that some patients have reported pain requiring sedation, that improper application may leave surface dents from uneven healing, and that fat necrosis and atrophic scarring have been reported.[8]

Thermage's introduction in 2002 started a market for non-ablative RF and electrical-energy devices that heat skin in a controlled way.[4] Pellevé followed using 4 MHz monopolar RF from Ellman International, of Oceanside, New York.[1][2] The Ellman system is also described in the French review under the Surgitron Dual RF S5 name.[7]

The 2012 17-patient facial series, the 2013 31-patient randomised-hand multicenter study, and the 2014 12-patient periorbital cohort are described above.[1][2][3] ClinicalTrials.gov lists a 40-participant study of single versus double and triple Pellevé therapy for facial wrinkles (started 2010), a 49-participant neck wrinkle study (2010) and an 89-participant study of an RF device for tissue heating and coagulation (2017); results for the registered studies are not summarised here.[5][6][9]
All published studies are small, and the facial and periorbital series did not describe a control arm.

timeline.event: Thermage introduced, beginning the market for non-ablative RF skin heating devices.[4]
Registered studies of single versus repeated Pellevé therapy for facial wrinkles and a neck wrinkle study begin; a French review describes the Ellman 4 MHz system.[5][6][7]
Clinical article describes the Pelleve procedure for wrinkle reduction and tightening.[4]

name: Pelleve

card.summary: Ellman's 4-MHz monopolar RF system for wrinkles and tightening, backed by small uncontrolled studies.
card.note: Studies are small and mostly without control groups.

quick.overview:
Pellevé is a clinic-based monopolar radiofrequency system from Ellman International used for facial and neck wrinkles and, in one study, hand wrinkles.
Published work is limited to small studies of 12 to 31 patients.
quick.mechanism: Continuous 4-MHz radiofrequency energy heats skin to therapeutic temperature, with the aim of contracting collagen and stimulating new collagen.
quick.risks: Little safety detail is available; category-wide RF reports include pain, burns, pigment change and rare scarring or fat loss.
